Our current hedge settings are 0% for rate hedges and 0% for equity hedges, so the tool shows no current hedge cost; it does not give a dollar estimate of loss if that dealer failed.

off.question: What is our biggest risk right now?
off.reply: Our biggest risk is falling interest rates: the rate mismatch (duration gap) is negative 3.59 years, so liabilities are more rate-sensitive than assets. A one-basis-point rate fall reduces surplus by $26.9 million; the dashboard marks this risk red. Liquidity is also tight at a 101.7% ratio against a 100% floor, while capital is stronger at 159.6%.

off.question: How much would our surplus change if interest rates fell by 1%?

facts.name: surplus change for a 1% fall ($bn, from net DV01)

off.reply: The dashboard estimates that each 1 bp rate fall reduces surplus by $26.9 million. Scaled to a 1% fall, that is an estimated $2.69 billion decrease, assuming the sensitivity scales proportionally. The rate mismatch (duration gap) is -3.59 years, which is why falling rates hurt surplus.

off.question: What is our capital ratio, and how close are we to the floor?
off.reply: Our capital ratio (simplified capital ratio) is 159.6%, which is 59.6 percentage points above the 100% floor. The dashboard marks capital green.

off.question: Should we hedge more of the stock-market guarantees?
off.reply: There is a case for adding some protection: equity puts currently hedge none of the guarantees, and a 10% stock fall would add $0.71 billion to guarantee costs before considering other company effects. Each extra 10% of put hedging costs $0.0085 billion per quarter, whether or not the protection pays; hedging more reduces that guarantee risk but does not remove the cost. I would treat this as a trade-off, not a prediction that stocks will fall; the figures here do not establish the best hedge level for the whole company.

off.question: Should we sell some junk and BBB bonds and buy government bonds?
off.reply: A shift toward government bonds is reasonable for liquidity and modestly helps capital, but it does not address our main flagged risk: the rate mismatch (duration gap). In the preview, the liquidity ratio rises from 101.7% to 131.4%, and the capital ratio from 159.6% to 160.6%; the surplus is unchanged. The trade-off is lower investment income: government bonds yield 3.31%, versus 4.09% for investment-grade corporates and 5.65% for below-investment-grade bonds. I would consider a measured shift, but not treat it as a substitute for addressing the rate mismatch; this is a preview, not a trade or a forecast.

off.question: Do we have enough cash on hand if policyholders start surrendering?
off.reply: Cash alone is not enough for the full 90-day stress: we have $5.7bn in cash against $8.54bn of stressed outflows. Including government bonds, stressed liquid assets are $8.69bn, just above those outflows; the liquidity ratio is 101.7%, only slightly above the 100% floor. In the projection with rates up 100bp and surrenders at 1.5× normal, extra surrender outflow is $1.07bn and is marked covered by cash. So we appear covered in the modeled stress, but the cushion is thin—not a comfortable buffer. [liquidity ratio]

off.question: What would a 10% fall in the stock market do to us?
off.reply: A hypothetical 10% stock-market fall would reduce our surplus by $0.79bn, with the change attributed to equity in the test. The test shows no change from rates, credit spreads, defaults, liquidity or counterparties. This is a what-if on today’s book, not a forecast of this quarter’s shock.

off.question: What would it cost per quarter to close half of our rate mismatch with swaps?
off.reply: Closing half of the rate mismatch (duration gap) means a 50% rate hedge. At the quoted cost of $0.004 billion per quarter for each extra 10% hedged, that would cost $0.020 billion per quarter. That is the hedge cost, not a trade ticket; no trade has been proposed or executed.

off.question: Should we add rate protection before the next quarter?
off.reply: There is a case for adding some rate protection: our rate mismatch (duration gap) is -3.59 years, and each basis point rates fall cuts surplus by $26.9 million. Each extra 10% of rate hedging costs $0.004 billion per quarter; it would cushion falling rates, but it would also lose value if rates rise. The inflation wire is only a hint, not a forecast, and liquidity is just above its 100% floor, so I would not add a large hedge based on that headline alone.

off.question: What happens to us if one of our derivatives dealers fails?
off.reply: Right now, we have no derivatives in place and no uncollateralized dealer exposure, so a dealer failure would not create a loss on an existing hedge. If we add hedges, a failed dealer might not pay what it owes us, and we could face a replacement cost to set up the hedge elsewhere; that is counterparty risk. Daily collateral can limit that loss, but it costs money, and using more dealers also adds cost.
